findings.title: The root account has MFA enabled

vanta.test: MFA is enabled on the root account

steps: Sign in to the AWS console as the root user (account email and password).
Open the account menu (top right) and go to Security credentials.
Under Multi-factor authentication (MFA) choose Assign MFA device.
Choose the device type. An authenticator app is enough for this check; Drata 225 needs a hardware key (see IAM-002).
Register the device with two consecutive codes and confirm.
Store the recovery access in a shared, protected place of the team (not in the repo or in a chat).
remediation.notes: The AWS CLI cannot enable MFA for the root user: it can only be done from the console as the root user.

findings.title: Plaintext credentials in the vault

steps: Revoke or rotate the exposed credential from the AWS console (IAM) before editing the note.
Remove the value from the vault note and keep a reference to the secrets manager in its place.
Review the history of the vault and of the repos that sync it for copies of the credential.
remediation.notes: A credential written in the vault must be treated as compromised.

findings.title: S3 buckets have Block Public Access on in all 4 settings
findings.vault_claim: The uploads bucket blocks all public access

vanta.test: Buckets use Block Public Access settings

steps: Check whether the bucket acme-notes-uploads serves public content on purpose (static website or public ACL) and, if so, put it behind CloudFront with private access before blocking.
Turn on the 4 Block Public Access settings on the bucket.
Verify with get-public-access-block that the 4 settings are true.
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
# read-only: whether the bucket is public according to its policy
aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket "acme-notes-uploads" --region "$REGION"

REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket "acme-notes-uploads" --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: No downtime, but if the bucket serves public content on purpose (static website with anonymous access, public ACLs), it stops being accessible: move it behind CloudFront with Origin Access Control first. get-bucket-policy-status answers NoSuchBucketPolicy if the bucket has no policy: that is not an error. Reversible with put-public-access-block set to false. The account-level Block Public Access (aws s3control put-public-access-block) is also recommended, but Drata does not evaluate it.

findings.title: Inventory resources have the VantaOwner tag with an owner's email

steps: Decide who owns acme-notes-assets: an active person in Vanta (not a shared mailbox or a deactivated user).
Set the VantaOwner tag to that person's email.
Verify that the tag shows up and wait for the next Vanta sync (roughly every hour).
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
RESOURCE_ARN="__FILL_IN_RESOURCE_ARN__"
OWNER_EMAIL="__FILL_IN_OWNER_EMAIL__"
aws resourcegroupstaggingapi tag-resources --resource-arn-list "$RESOURCE_ARN" --tags "VantaOwner=$OWNER_EMAIL" --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: __FILL_IN_RESOURCE_ARN__ is the ARN of the resource acme-notes-assets, taken from the inventory. tag-resources adds or overwrites only the given tags and leaves the rest (S3 put-bucket-tagging replaces all of them). For an S3 bucket use the bucket's region in REGION. No downtime. Vanta only reads the tags, it never writes them. The email must match an active Vanta user: otherwise the resource is left without an owner even if this check passes. If the team uses another tag name for the owner (for example owner), Vanta lets you map it to VantaOwner in Settings, but this check looks for VantaOwner. tag-resources reports failures in FailedResourcesMap: review it.

findings.title: No security group in a region with active network interfaces opens SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0

vanta.test: No security group allows unrestricted IPv4 ingress to remote administration ports
No security group allows unrestricted IPv6 ingress (::/0) to remote administration ports

steps: Identify who connects through SSH to the security group sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718 today (detail.ip_permissions of the finding and the VPC Flow Logs) and first enable an alternative access: Session Manager, or a rule with a fixed CIDR (the office or VPN IP) or with another security group as the source.

Revoke the offending rules with the command: it uses the exact JSON of detail.ip_permissions of this finding (protocol, ports and only the offending CIDRs), so it does not touch any other rule of the group.
Verify with describe-security-groups that no inbound rule open to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 is left on the port.
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
SG_ID="sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718"
# detail.ip_permissions: only the offending rules of this finding, with their exact protocol, ports and CIDRs
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --ip-permissions '[{"IpProtocol":"tcp","FromPort":22,"ToPort":22,"IpRanges":[{"CidrIp":"0.0.0.0/0"}]}]'
remediation.notes: Revoking is immediate and reversible with authorize-security-group-ingress. Risk: cutting the access of whoever connects from the internet today; open the alternative access first. The command uses revoke-security-group-ingress with --ip-permissions '[{"IpProtocol":"tcp","FromPort":22,"ToPort":22,"IpRanges":[{"CidrIp":"0.0.0.0/0"}]}]', which is filled in with the exact JSON of the offending rules (stable key detail.ip_permissions: IpProtocol, FromPort, ToPort and only the offending CIDRs): if a rule does not match, AWS answers InvalidPermission.NotFound and changes nothing, and the other rules of the group are never revoked. A rule with a range (for example 0-65535) or with protocol -1 also opens other ports: revoking it closes all of them, review detail.ip_permissions. Prefix lists are not expanded: if a prefix list contains 0.0.0.0/0, this check does not see it. The Drata article says a specific CIDR does not count as a pass for test 102: if it keeps failing with specific CIDRs, prefer Session Manager or a security group as the source.

findings.title: A multi-region CloudTrail trail exists and is logging (IsLogging=true)
findings.vault_claim: A multi-region trail is missing; pending a ticket

vanta.test: CloudTrail is enabled in all regions

steps: Decide the trail name and the S3 bucket where the logs are stored (a bucket dedicated to logs, with versioning and a bucket policy that lets CloudTrail write; see LOG-006).
If no trail exists, create a multi-region one with file validation and start it with start-logging.
If the trail already exists but is stopped, start it again with start-logging.
Confirm with get-trail-status that IsLogging is true and that there are no delivery errors.
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
TRAIL_NAME="__FILL_IN_TRAIL_NAME__"
LOG_BUCKET="__FILL_IN_LOGS_BUCKET__"
# create-trail does not start logging: start-logging only runs if the trail was created
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name "$TRAIL_NAME" --s3-bucket-name "$LOG_BUCKET" --is-multi-region-trail --include-global-service-events --enable-log-file-validation --region "$REGION" && aws cloudtrail start-logging --name "$TRAIL_NAME" --region "$REGION"

REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
TRAIL_NAME="__FILL_IN_TRAIL_NAME__"
# only if the trail already exists and is stopped
aws cloudtrail start-logging --name "$TRAIL_NAME" --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: The bucket must first have the bucket policy that lets cloudtrail.amazonaws.com write; without it create-trail fails with InsufficientS3BucketPolicyException. The first copy of management events is free; additional trails and data events are charged. Decision: trail name and destination bucket. If the trail already exists under another name, use the second block.

findings.title: RDS instances have automated backups with retention greater than 0 days (recommended: at least 7)

steps: Choose the retention (7 days is the recommended minimum) for the account database.
Apply it with the first block (standalone instance) or with the second (member of an Aurora cluster or Multi-AZ DB cluster, where retention belongs to the cluster).
Verify with describe-db-instances that BackupRetentionPeriod is the chosen one.
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
DB_ID="account"
# instance that does not belong to a cluster
aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --backup-retention-period 7 --apply-immediately --region "$REGION"

REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
DB_ID="account"
# cluster member: retention is changed on the cluster
CLUSTER_ID=$(aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'DBInstances[0].DBClusterIdentifier' --output text)
[ -n "$CLUSTER_ID" ] && [ "$CLUSTER_ID" != "None" ] && aws rds modify-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID" --backup-retention-period 7 --apply-immediately --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: Going from 0 to a higher value interrupts the database for a few minutes on a Single-AZ instance (RDS takes a snapshot and suspends I/O); raising from a value above 0 to 7 does not. Apply it in an agreed window. Backups cost storage beyond the size of the database. --apply-immediately also applies any other pending change of the instance. A read replica without backups also fails this test. 7 days is a catalog design criterion, not a Drata threshold (which only asks for more than 0): that is why 1 to 6 is reported with severity_override low.

findings.title: GuardDuty is active in every region with resources (regions without resources and without a detector are reported with low severity)

steps: Enable GuardDuty in the us-east-1 region with S3 Protection on, running the command in that region.
If the region already has a disabled detector, create-detector fails: re-enable it with update-detector (second block).
Verify with get-detector that Status is ENABLED.
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
# fails with BadRequestException if the region already has a detector: use the next block
aws guardduty create-detector --enable --region "us-east-1" --features '[{"Name":"S3_DATA_EVENTS","Status":"ENABLED"}]'

REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
# only if the region already has a disabled detector
DETECTOR_ID=$(aws guardduty list-detectors --region "$REGION" --query 'DetectorIds[0]' --output text) && aws guardduty update-detector --detector-id "$DETECTOR_ID" --enable --features '[{"Name":"S3_DATA_EVENTS","Status":"ENABLED"}]' --region "$REGION"
remediation.verify_after: aws guardduty get-detector --detector-id "$(aws guardduty list-detectors --region "us-east-1" --query 'DetectorIds[0]' --output text)" --region "us-east-1" --query '{Status: Status, S3: Features[?Name==`S3_DATA_EVENTS`].Status | [0]}'
remediation.notes: No downtime. Cost: 30 days free trial, then GuardDuty charges by the volume of events analyzed (CloudTrail, flow logs, DNS and, with S3 Protection, S3 data events); in a region with no activity the cost is minimal. Findings for regions without resources have low severity: enabling them anyway closes the gap of unmonitored regions that the AWS security baseline recommends. The detector is per region: repeat the command in each offending region.

findings.title: No security group in a region with active network interfaces has an 'all traffic' inbound rule from a CIDR

steps: Decide which ports, protocols and sources the security group sg-0f1e2d3c4b5a69788 needs and first open those specific rules with authorize-security-group-ingress, so as not to cut legitimate traffic.
Revoke the 'all traffic' rules from CIDRs with the command: it uses the exact JSON of detail.ip_permissions of this finding, so it does not touch any other rule of the group.
Verify that the group no longer has inbound rules with protocol -1 from a CIDR.
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
SG_ID="sg-0f1e2d3c4b5a69788"
# detail.ip_permissions: only the offending rules of this finding, with their exact protocol, ports and CIDRs
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --ip-permissions __FILL_IN_IP_PERMISSIONS__
remediation.notes: This is the 'all traffic' rule: revoking it cuts everything that depended on it, so the specific rules must be opened first, for example: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <sg> --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr <range> --region <region>. The command uses --ip-permissions __FILL_IN_IP_PERMISSIONS__, which is filled in with the exact JSON of the -1 rules with a CIDR of this group (stable key detail.ip_permissions); rules with another protocol or with a source security group are not touched, and if a rule does not match AWS answers InvalidPermission.NotFound without changing anything. Revoking is reversible with authorize-security-group-ingress.

findings.title: Customer-managed policies do not use broad wildcards without justification (review)

drata.name: AWS IAM Principle of Least Privilege

steps: Read the policy with the commands below and list which wildcard actions it uses and on which resources.
Replace each wildcard with the list of actions and resources the application really needs.
Create a new version of the policy and check that the application keeps working.
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
POLICY_ARN="__FILL_IN_POLICY_ARN__"
VERSION_ID=$(aws iam get-policy --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" --query Policy.DefaultVersionId --output text)
aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" --version-id "$VERSION_ID"
remediation.notes: This is a judgment review (done by Claude, not a fixed rule): a wildcard can be acceptable. Narrowing permissions without testing breaks the application that uses them.

findings.title: S3 buckets have Block Public Access on in all 4 settings

vanta.test: Buckets use Block Public Access settings

steps: Check whether the bucket acme-notes-uploads serves public content on purpose (static website or public ACL) and, if so, put it behind CloudFront with private access before blocking.
Turn on the 4 Block Public Access settings on the bucket.
Verify with get-public-access-block that the 4 settings are true.
commands:
REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
# read-only: whether the bucket is public according to its policy
aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket "acme-notes-uploads" --region "$REGION"

REGION="us-east-1"
ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket "acme-notes-uploads" --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: No downtime, but if the bucket serves public content on purpose (static website with anonymous access, public ACLs), it stops being accessible: move it behind CloudFront with Origin Access Control first. get-bucket-policy-status answers NoSuchBucketPolicy if the bucket has no policy: that is not an error. Reversible with put-public-access-block set to false. The account-level Block Public Access (aws s3control put-public-access-block) is also recommended, but Drata does not evaluate it.
